catalog_quote: Regarding the vocabulary below the following explanation is necessary: a, e, i, o, u, are pronounced as in Spanish. ö, as in German Löwe. ts, as German z in Zeit. x, as English sh in she. ch, as in Spanish. All other letters as in English. The stress accent is on the last syllable unless otherwise indicated (´). v and f occur in only a few words and are by some people pronounced like b and p respectively. [...] The following vocabulary was taken in different parts of the department of Yoro, but the same language is spoken by the entire Eastern branch. The words enclosed in parenthesis are the corresponding names in the language of the Western branch. From a comparison of the two, it will readily be seen that these languages are mutually intelligible and that they are in reality dialects of the same language. new_statements.rule_in_words: In Conzemius's field vocabulary of Jicaque (Eastern forms with Western-branch equivalents in parentheses), word stress is on the final syllable by default; the minority of words with non-final stress are marked with an acute accent (e.g. Western búa 'jaguar'). I.e. predominantly final stress with lexically marked exceptions, stated as a transcription convention rather than as an analysed rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Non-final stress 'otherwise indicated' by an acute on individual items; in the list e.g. búa / Western (búa) 'jaguar', búa he 'puma', hoyóro 'kidney', krátsa 'cockroach'.
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms in an elicited wordlist (c. 1921 fieldwork); the convention covers both the Eastern (Yoro) headwords and the parenthesised Western (Chamelecón/Villanueva, Cortés) forms. No phrase-level information. Later descriptions of the Eastern sister variety disagree (Von Hagen 1943:81 mostly antepenult; Fleming & Dennis 1977:127 final if consonant-final, penult if vowel-final), so the fixed: final syllable reading for Western Jicaque rests on this one early source.
new_statements.identity_note: Conzemius 1923 describes the 'western tribe' of the Jicaques living 'in the vicinity of the pueblos Chamelecon and Villanueva, Department of Cortés.. near extinction, not exceeding a population of 100' -- this is Glottolog's Western Jicaque (west2777, El Palmar near Chamelecón, Cortés). His vocabulary is primarily Eastern Jicaque (Tol, toll1241) taken 'in different parts of the department of Yoro'; Western-branch forms are given in parentheses after the Eastern ones, and the transcription note (default final stress, exceptions marked with an acute) governs the whole list, Western forms included (e.g. Western búa 'jaguar' carries a marked non-final accent). So the statement is a wordlist transcription convention covering both varieties, not a Western-only phonological analysis. Note the Eastern variety has divergent later descriptions (Von Hagen 1943:81 'accent follows no definite rule; most words.. ante-penultimate' for Montaña de la Flor; Fleming & Dennis 1977:127 final if C-final, penult if V-final), which lowers confidence in a plain fixed: final syllable reading.

sources.note: p.81 (own Montaña de la Flor = Eastern/Tol data): 'accent. Follows no definite rule; most words, however, are accented on the ante-penultimate syllable. In the verbal infinitive, the accentuation is the penultimate. In bi-syllabic words, the accent falls on the first syllable.' Nothing on accent for the El Palmar (Western) vocabulary, which he only discusses second-hand from Membreño (pp.79-80: 'most inaccurate transcription').
